summary.text: Since $2^{58n+26}\equiv204\pmod{233}$, while $2^{233}\equiv1\pmod{1399}$ and $2^{206}\equiv-3\pmod{1399}$, the target number is always divisible by $1399$. For every smaller prime, Fermat reduction makes the relevant exponent periodic in $n$, and finite residue checks exclude divisibility except that $67,271,523$ can occur only for $n\equiv2\pmod5$, $n\equiv11\pmod{18}$, $n\equiv26\pmod{42}$ respectively; these congruences force coverage by Conjectures 1–3, so the hypotheses exclude them and make $1399$ the least prime factor.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(k)=2^{2^k+2}+3,
\qquad a(k)=\text{the least prime factor of }F(k).
\]
Fix \(n\geq 0\), put
\[
k=58n+26,
\qquad N=F(k)=2^{2^{58n+26}+2}+3,
\]
and suppose that \(k\) is not covered by any of Conjectures 1–3. Explicitly, our hypothesis is that none of the following holds:

1. \(k=10m+2\) for some \(m\geq0\);
2. \(k=36m+16\) for some \(m\geq0\) with \(m\not\equiv1\pmod5\);
3. \(k=84m+22\) for some \(m\geq0\) with \(m\not\equiv0\pmod5\).

We prove that the least prime factor of \(N\) is \(1399\).

## 1. A periodic modular reduction

We first record the general reduction used to exclude primes below \(1399\). For a positive integer \(q\), define
\[
c(r)=58r+26,
\qquad e_q(r)=\bigl(2^{c(r)}+2\bigr)\bmod(q-1),
\]
where the remainder is chosen in \(\{0,1,\ldots,q-2\}\).

Suppose that \(T>0\) and that, for every \(r\) with \(0\leq r<T\),
\[
2^{c(r)}2^{58T}\equiv 2^{c(r)}\pmod{q-1}. \tag{1}
\]
Then for every \(t\geq0\), induction on \(t\) gives
\[
2^{58Tt+c(r)}\equiv2^{c(r)}\pmod{q-1}. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, the assertion is immediate for \(t=0\), and multiplication by \(2^{58T}\), followed by (1), proves the induction step.

Given any \(n\), write \(n=Tt+r\), where \(0\leq r<T\). Since
\[
58n+26=58Tt+c(r),
\]
formula (2) yields
\[
2^{58n+26}\equiv2^{c(r)}\pmod{q-1}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^{58n+26}+2\equiv e_q(r)\pmod{q-1}. \tag{3}
\]
If \(q\) is prime, Fermat's theorem gives \(2^{q-1}\equiv1\pmod q\). Reducing the outer exponent in \(N\) by (3), we therefore obtain
\[
N=2^{2^{58n+26}+2}+3
   \equiv 2^{e_q(r)}+3\pmod q. \tag{4}
\]
Thus, if in addition
\[
2^{e_q(r)}+3\not\equiv0\pmod q
\quad(0\leq r<T), \tag{5}
\]
then \(q\nmid N\) for every \(n\).

All modular powers in what follows are evaluated by repeated squaring. To make the finite calculation precise and reproducible, for each displayed pair \(q:T\), one computes, for \(0\leq r<T\),
\[
u_r=2^{58r+26}\bmod(q-1),\qquad
v=2^{58T}\bmod(q-1),
\]
checks \(u_rv\equiv u_r\pmod{q-1}\), then computes
\[
2^{(u_r+2)\bmod(q-1)}+3\pmod q
\]
and checks that it is nonzero. These are exactly conditions (1) and (5).

For every pair in this table, the two finite checks just described establish (1) and (5). Hence (4) proves that none of these primes divides \(N\).

The remaining prime \(2\) does not divide \(N\), because \(2^{58n+26}+2>0\), so \(2^{2^{58n+26}+2}\) is even, while adding \(3\) makes \(N\) odd.

It remains to handle \(67,271,523\). For these primes the finite calculation does find a zero, but only in residue classes that force one of the three coverage conditions.

## 2. The exceptional prime \(67\)

For \(q=67\), use \(T=5\). Direct modular exponentiation gives, for every \(0\leq r<5\),
\[
2^{58r+26}2^{58\cdot5}\equiv2^{58r+26}\pmod{66}.
\]
The finite list of outer residues has the following decisive property:
\[
2^{e_{67}(r)}+3\equiv0\pmod{67}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=2. \tag{6}
\]
By the periodic reduction, if \(67\mid N\), then with \(r=n\bmod5\), the left side of (6) vanishes. Hence
\[
n\equiv2\pmod5.
\]
Write \(n=5s+2\). Then
\[
k=58n+26=58(5s+2)+26=290s+142=10(29s+14)+2.
\]
Thus \(k\) is covered by Conjecture 1. Under our noncoverage hypothesis this is impossible, so \(67\nmid N\).

## 3. The exceptional prime \(271\)

For \(q=271\), use \(T=18\). The corresponding finite calculations are
\[
2^{58r+26}2^{58\cdot18}\equiv2^{58r+26}\pmod{270}
\quad(0\leq r<18),
\]
and
\[
2^{e_{271}(r)}+3\equiv0\pmod{271}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=11. \tag{7}
\]
Therefore \(271\mid N\) implies \(n\equiv11\pmod{18}\). Write
\[
n=18s+11.
\]
A direct rearrangement gives
\[
k=58n+26=58(18s+11)+26
  =1044s+664
  =36(29s+18)+16. \tag{8}
\]
Set \(m=29s+18\). If \(m\not\equiv1\pmod5\), equation (8) says exactly that \(k\) is covered by Conjecture 2.

There is one remaining case, \(m\equiv1\pmod5\). Since
\[
m=29s+18\equiv4s+3\pmod5,
\]
this congruence gives \(4s+3\equiv1\pmod5\), hence \(s\equiv2\pmod5\). It follows that
\[
n=18s+11\equiv3s+1\equiv3\cdot2+1\equiv2\pmod5.
\]
As in the preceding section, \(n\equiv2\pmod5\) implies
\(k=10(29((n-2)/5)+14)+2\), so \(k\) is covered by Conjecture 1.

Thus in every case \(271\mid N\) forces coverage by Conjecture 1 or Conjecture 2. Our hypothesis excludes both, and consequently \(271\nmid N\).

## 4. The exceptional prime \(523\)

For \(q=523\), use \(T=42\). Direct modular exponentiation gives
\[
2^{58r+26}2^{58\cdot42}\equiv2^{58r+26}\pmod{522}
\quad(0\leq r<42),
\]
and the only possible zero is
\[
2^{e_{523}(r)}+3\equiv0\pmod{523}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=26. \tag{9}
\]
Therefore \(523\mid N\) implies \(n\equiv26\pmod{42}\). Write
\[
n=42s+26.
\]
Then
\[
k=58n+26=58(42s+26)+26
  =2436s+1534
  =84(29s+18)+22. \tag{10}
\]
Again put \(m=29s+18\). If \(m\not\equiv0\pmod5\), (10) shows that \(k\) is covered by Conjecture 3.

If instead \(m\equiv0\pmod5\), then
\[
4s+3\equiv0\pmod5,
\]
so \(s\equiv3\pmod5\). Hence
\[
n=42s+26\equiv2s+1\equiv2\cdot3+1\equiv2\pmod5.
\]
This once more implies that \(k\) is covered by Conjecture 1.

Thus \(523\mid N\) forces coverage by Conjecture 1 or Conjecture 3. The noncoverage hypothesis excludes these alternatives, so \(523\nmid N\).

Combining the table, the parity argument, and the three exceptional cases, we have proved:

> No prime less than \(1399\) divides \(N\).

## 5. Divisibility by \(1399\)

We now prove that \(1399\) itself always divides \(N\), without any noncoverage assumption.

First, repeated squaring gives the three explicit congruences
\[
2^{58}\equiv1\pmod{233},\qquad
2^{26}\equiv204\pmod{233}, \tag{11}
\]
\[
2^{233}\equiv1\pmod{1399}, \tag{12}
\]
and
\[
2^{206}\equiv-3\pmod{1399}. \tag{13}
\]
From (11),
\[
2^{58n+26}=(2^{58})^n2^{26}\equiv204\pmod{233}. \tag{14}
\]
Let \(E=2^{58n+26}\). Equation (14) says that \(E=233h+204\) for some integer \(h\geq0\), and therefore
\[
E+2=233h+206.
\]
Using (12) and then (13),
\[
2^{E+2}+3
 =2^{233h+206}+3
 =(2^{233})^h2^{206}+3
 \equiv2^{206}+3
 \equiv0\pmod{1399}.
\]
Thus
\[
1399\mid N. \tag{15}
\]

For completeness, the explicit congruences (11)–(13) are ordinary short repeated-squaring computations: starting with \(2\), successively square modulo the indicated modulus to obtain the residues of \(2^{1},2^{2},2^{4},\ldots\), and multiply the residues corresponding to the binary digits of \(58,26,233,206\). Their role is respectively to make the inner exponent constant modulo \(233\), to give period \(233\) for the outer power modulo \(1399\), and to produce the final residue \(-3\).

## 6. Identification of the least prime factor

The number \(N\) is greater than \(1\), so it has a least prime factor. By (15), its least prime factor is at most \(1399\). On the other hand, every prime divisor of \(N\) is at least \(1399\), because all primes below \(1399\) were excluded in Sections 1–4. Hence the least prime factor is at least \(1399\). The two inequalities give
\[
a(58n+26)=\operatorname{lpf}(N)=1399.
\]
This holds for every \(n\geq0\) for which the index \(58n+26\) is not covered by Conjectures 1–3, as required.
